conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. I’ve been having this awful pain in my left side—burning and stabbing. It’s been getting worse since I got out of the hospital two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how bad is the pain on a scale from 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was a 13 earlier—like, off the charts. My wife found me passed out in the shower today. That’s when she brought me in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for telling me. We’ve reviewed your records. You were just discharged two days ago for similar symptoms. Did the pain go away when you left?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it was still there. They said I was okay to go, but it got worse fast. I couldn’t eat, couldn’t take my meds. Just kept throwing up—little specks of blood in it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve given you some fluids and pain medicine through the IV. Your labs came back—no sign of infection or pancreas flare-up. The CT scan shows your chronic pancreatitis, but no new blockages or complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an emergency? But the pain feels serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious because it’s affecting your life. But we don’t see anything surgically urgent. The pain is likely from your chronic pancreatitis, possibly made worse by stress and not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been having bad dreams—seeing dead people. And sometimes I hear my mom calling me. I know she’s not really there, but it scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really distressing. You mentioned you stopped some of your psychiatric meds—ziprasidone, gabapentin, and cymbalta—after your last stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they told me to hold off. But since then, the nightmares got worse. I’m scared something bad will happen to my kids or me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve asked psychiatry to see you. They recommend restarting gabapentin and ziprasidone, and adding prazosin for the nightmares. They also suggest stopping amitriptyline—it might be making you dizzy or lightheaded, which could contribute to passing out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to feel better. And I really need to get home soon—I haven’t seen my kids in five months. Father’s Day is coming up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that. We’ll do our best to get you stable so you can go home. For now, you’re on IV fluids and pain meds. We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m thirsty. Can I have water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to make sure your stomach is ready. We’ll start with clear liquids tomorrow if your nausea improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, doc. I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain’s down to a 4 with the meds. I’m still bloated and a little nauseous, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Your labs are stable. We’re going to start you on clear liquids—apple juice, broth. If you tolerate that, we’ll move to soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have Gatorade? That’s all I’ve been drinking at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can give you that. And we’ll switch your pain medicine from IV to oral hydromorphone so you can manage it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? I haven’t taken anything since I left the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding metformin while you’re not eating, but we’ll restart it before you go home. Omeprazole and lisinopril are safe to continue. Aspirin too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new ones—prazosin and ziprasidone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Psychiatry recommends starting prazosin at night for nightmares, and ziprasidone twice daily. Gabapentin three times a day. We’ll stop amitriptyline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will ziprasidone make me gain weight? I’ve had that problem before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, but your psychiatrist thinks the benefits outweigh the risks. They also mentioned possibly trying an SSRI later, but carefully, because of your bipolar history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to sleep without seeing those faces.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down apple juice and broth. We’re going to advance you to a soft diet—mashed potatoes, toast. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s around a 3. I’m still tender on the left side, but not like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And no more passing out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not since the shower. My blood pressure okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not orthostatic—your BP stays stable when you sit up. The syncope was likely vasovagal, triggered by pain and stress. Controlling the pain helps prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on regular food for a few hours with no nausea or pain flare. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! I can see my kids for Father’s Day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll give you prescriptions: prazosin, ziprasidone, gabapentin, and ondansetron for nausea. Restart metformin, omeprazole, lisinopril, and aspirin. Stop amitriptyline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my enzyme pills for the pancreas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking those with meals. And follow up with your primary doctor and Community Counseling. They’ll get your records from this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your wife is here. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Thank you, doc. I feel a lot better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, eat small meals, and call if the pain comes back or you pass out again. Have a great Father’s Day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.
